title: No. 8 — The Consequences of Hostilities Between the States (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Taking it as established, then, that the several States—if disunited, or thrown into whatever combinations might emerge from the wreck of the general Confederacy—would be subject to the same alternations of peace and war, friendship and hostility with each other that have been the lot of all neighboring nations not united under one government, let us briefly examine some of the consequences such a situation would bring.

War between the States, in the early period of their separate existence, would bring far greater suffering than it usually does in countries that have long had regular military establishments. The disciplined armies always kept up on the European continent, while bearing a malign aspect to liberty and economy, have nonetheless produced the considerable benefit of making sudden conquests impractical and preventing the rapid devastation that used to mark the progress of war before such armies existed. The art of fortification has contributed to the same ends. The nations of Europe are ringed with chains of fortified places that mutually obstruct invasion. Campaigns are spent reducing two or three frontier garrisons just to gain entrance into an enemy's country. Similar obstacles arise at every step to wear down the strength and slow the advance of an invader. Once, an invading army would penetrate to the heart of a neighboring country almost as quickly as news of its approach could be received. Now a comparatively small force of disciplined troops, acting on the defensive with the help of fortifications, can impede and ultimately frustrate the efforts of a much larger one. The history of war in that part of the globe is no longer a history of nations subdued and empires overturned, but of towns taken and retaken; of battles that decide nothing; of retreats more useful than victories; of much effort and little gain.

In this country the picture would be entirely reversed. Suspicion of military establishments would put them off as long as possible. The lack of fortifications, leaving the frontiers of one State open to another, would invite incursions. The populous States would, with little trouble, overrun their less populous neighbors. Conquests would be as easy to make as they would be hard to keep. War, therefore, would be erratic and predatory. PLUNDER and devastation always march in the train of irregular forces. The sufferings of individuals would be the leading feature of the events that defined our military exploits.

This picture is not overdrawn—though I admit it would not long remain accurate. Safety from external danger is the most powerful guide of national conduct. Even the ardent love of liberty will, after a while, give way to its demands. The violent destruction of life and property that goes with war, and the constant strain and alarm of a state of continual danger, will compel even the nations most attached to liberty to turn for repose and security to institutions that tend to destroy their civil and political rights. To be safer, they eventually become willing to risk being less free.

The institutions chiefly meant here are STANDING ARMIES and the related apparatus of military establishments. Standing armies, it is said, are not provided against in the new Constitution, and so it is inferred that they may exist under it.(1) Their existence, however, by the very terms of the proposition, is at most uncertain and conditional. But standing armies, one may reply, must inevitably follow from a dissolution of the Confederacy. Frequent war and constant apprehension, which require an equally constant state of preparation, will reliably produce them. The weaker States or confederacies would resort to them first, to put themselves on a level with their more powerful neighbors. They would try to make up for inferior population and resources by a more regular and effective system of defense, by disciplined troops, and by fortifications. At the same time, they would be forced to strengthen the executive arm of government, and in doing so their constitutions would gradually drift toward monarchy. It is in the nature of war to enlarge the executive at the expense of legislative authority.

The measures just described would soon give the States or confederacies that adopted them a superiority over their neighbors. Small states, or states of less natural strength, with vigorous governments and the help of disciplined armies, have often triumphed over large states, or states of greater natural strength, that lacked these advantages. Neither the pride nor the safety of the more important States or confederacies would let them long submit to this humiliating and accidental superiority. They would quickly take up means similar to those by which it had been achieved, to recover their lost preeminence. So in a short time we would see established in every part of this country the same engines of despotism that have been the scourge of the Old World. This, at any rate, would be the natural course of things, and our reasoning will be the more sound the more it is fitted to that standard.

These are not vague inferences drawn from supposed or speculative defects in a Constitution whose entire power is lodged in the hands of a people, or their representatives and delegates. They are solid conclusions, drawn from the natural and necessary progress of human affairs.

It may perhaps be asked, by way of objection, why standing armies did not arise out of the disputes that so often distracted the ancient republics of Greece. Several answers, all equally satisfactory, can be given. The industrious habits of people today—absorbed in the pursuit of gain and devoted to the advancement of agriculture and commerce—are incompatible with the condition of a nation of soldiers, which was the actual condition of the people of those republics. The means of revenue, vastly multiplied by the increase of gold and silver and of industry, and the science of finance—an offspring of modern times—together with the habits of nations, have produced a complete revolution in the system of war and have made disciplined armies, distinct from the body of the citizens, the inseparable companions of frequent hostility.

There is also a wide difference between military establishments in a country rarely exposed by its situation to internal invasion, and in one that is often subject to such invasion and always afraid of it. The rulers of the first kind have no plausible pretext—even if they were inclined—to keep up armies as numerous as must necessarily be maintained in the second. Since these armies are seldom if ever called into activity for internal defense, the people are in no danger of being broken to military subordination. The laws are not accustomed to relaxing for military emergencies. The civil state remains in full vigor, neither corrupted nor confused by the principles or tendencies of the military state. The smallness of the army means the natural strength of the community more than matches it. And the citizens, not used to looking up to military power for protection or submitting to its oppressions, neither love nor fear the soldiery. They view them with a spirit of wary acquiescence as a necessary evil, and stand ready to resist a power they suspect may be turned against their rights.

An army under such conditions can usefully help the magistrate suppress a small faction, an occasional mob, or an insurrection. But it will be unable to enforce encroachments against the united efforts of the great body of the people.

In a country in the second predicament described above, the opposite of all this happens. The constant threat of danger forces the government to be always ready to repel it. Its armies must be numerous enough for immediate defense. The continual need for their services raises the importance of the soldier and proportionally lowers the condition of the citizen. The military state becomes elevated above the civil. The inhabitants of territories that are often the theater of war are unavoidably subjected to frequent infringements on their rights, which weaken their sense of those rights. By degrees, the people are brought to consider the soldiery not only as their protectors but as their superiors. The transition from this attitude to regarding them as masters is neither remote nor difficult. But it is very difficult to get a people in such a frame of mind to mount a bold or effective resistance to usurpations backed by military power.

The kingdom of Great Britain falls within the first description. An island situation and a powerful navy, guarding it largely against the possibility of foreign invasion, remove the need for a large army within the kingdom. Enough force to hold off a sudden landing until the militia could rally and form up has been all that was deemed necessary. No motive of national policy has demanded, nor would public opinion have tolerated, a larger number of troops on its home establishment. For a long time there has been little room for the operation of the other causes mentioned as the consequences of internal war. This peculiar good fortune of situation has gone a long way toward preserving the liberty that country still enjoys today, despite the prevailing venality and corruption. If, on the contrary, Britain had been situated on the continent and had been forced—as she would have been by that situation—to make her military establishments at home as large as those of the other great powers of Europe, she, like them, would in all probability today be a victim to the absolute power of a single man. It is possible, though not easy, that the people of that island may yet be enslaved from other causes; but it cannot be by the prowess of an army as small as the one usually kept up within the kingdom.

If we are wise enough to preserve the Union, we may for ages enjoy an advantage similar to that of an island situation. Europe is far from us. Her colonies in our vicinity are likely to remain too disproportioned in strength to threaten us seriously. Extensive military establishments cannot, in this position, be necessary to our security. But if we should be disunited, and the parts either stayed separated or—what is more likely—were thrown together into two or three confederacies, we would in a short time be in the predicament of the continental powers of Europe. Our liberties would fall prey to the means of defending ourselves against each other's ambition and jealousy.

This is no shallow or trivial idea, but a solid and weighty one. It deserves the most serious and careful consideration of every prudent and honest man, of whatever party. If such men will make a firm and solemn pause and reflect calmly on the importance of this idea; if they contemplate it in all its bearings and trace it to all its consequences, they will not hesitate to part with trivial objections to a Constitution whose rejection would in all likelihood put a final end to the Union. The airy phantoms that flit before the disordered imaginations of some of its opponents would quickly give way to the more substantial forms of dangers that are real, certain, and formidable.
